title: The Beatitudes, once more
hookLine: the poor, the mourners, the meek, the merciful: blessed
tomorrow: a strict rule or no rule at all: which one actually lasts?

cards: Hashtag blessed usually rides under a vacation photo, a new car, a promotion. Jesus's list of the blessed starts somewhere else: the poor in spirit, they that mourn, the meek. How can grief be blessed?
That sounds like the kind of thing you'd never say at a funeral. The answer starts with who was sitting on that hillside.

teach.b: Just before the sermon, Matthew lists the people brought to Jesus: the sick, people in torment of body and mind, people with palsy. He healed them, Matthew says, and crowds followed.
Then he sees them, goes up the mountain, sits down, and his first word is a word over them.

"Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. Blessed are they that mourn: for they shall be comforted. Blessed are the meek: for they shall inherit the earth." There's the answer to the puzzle.
The list doesn't tell anyone to go looking for poverty or grief.
It looks at people already hurting, people the world tends to pass over, and speaks a blessing with a promise attached: comforted, filled, shown mercy.
Then the grammar turns. All along it's been they. Near the end: "Blessed are ye."
Not a crowd in the distance.
You, the ones sitting here. Christians read the list in more than one way. Some hear a portrait of Jesus himself, meek and merciful.
Some hear a promise to the hurting. Some hear a call, the life his followers grow into. Some hold all three.
However it's read, the order stays the same: the blessing comes first, before anyone on that hillside has done a thing to earn it.

how: Churches read the Beatitudes in worship, and some Christians pray through them slowly, one line at a time, as a way of looking at their own lives.

o: rules for entering heaven, listed in order
songs the crowd sang on the way up the mountain
blessings Jesus spoke over the hurting and overlooked

p: theirs is the kingdom of heaven

s: 'blessed' in the Beatitudes means lucky, rich or doing well
the list blesses the poor in spirit, the mourners and the meek, with promises: comforted, filled, shown mercy.
Matthew says Jesus healed the crowds before the sermon began
Matthew 4:24–25: the sick and suffering were brought to him, and he healed them.
the Beatitudes tell people to go looking for grief and poverty
they speak a blessing over people already hurting; nobody is told to seek it.

games.q: you're on the hillside, sick and tired, hearing 'blessed are the meek.' then the grammar turns. who's blessed now?
o: only the disciples in the front row.
people in some faraway future age.
games.why: Matthew 5:11: 'Blessed are ye.' after a list of they, the blessing turns to the people sitting in front of him.

practice: Find a photo of someone easy to pass over, or someone carrying grief right now, and look at it for a while.
Hold them the way the list holds the mourners and the meek, and say over them the word Jesus used, blessed, or simply wish them good and mean it.

wordCard.voice: The Beatitudes. Blessings spoken over the poor in spirit, the mourners, the meek and the merciful, before anyone has earned a thing.

orig.note: Greek: blessed (plural). the first word of Matthew 5:3, and of each line after it.

carryVoice: Your line: blessed. On the mountain, the list ends by turning to the people listening. See you tomorrow.

sources.q: Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. Blessed are they that mourn: for they shall be comforted. Blessed are the meek: for they shall inherit the earth.
